name: Straw phonation

card.summary: Voicing through a narrow straw, a voice-therapy exercise with real clinical research, though not tested for vocal attractiveness.
card.aka: Semi-occluded vocal tract (SOVT) exercise; phonation into a straw
card.note: Studies concern voice quality and vocal fatigue in singers and patients, not perceived attractiveness.

quick.overview:
Straw phonation means making voiced sound while blowing through a narrow straw, which partly closes the vocal tract. It belongs to a family of semi-occluded vocal tract (SOVT) exercises used by voice teachers and speech-language pathologists, and some online voice-improvement communities have adopted it as a warm-up.

Published studies have examined its immediate effects and short therapy programmes in singers and people with voice disorders. Results are mostly short-term and in small samples, and none targets appearance or perceived attractiveness.
quick.mechanism: Narrowing the opening at the lips or straw changes air pressure and airflow in the vocal tract and at the vocal folds. Imaging and aerodynamic studies in singers have measured changes in vocal tract shape and glottal function during and after the exercise.[1][4]
quick.risks: The reviewed studies do not report notable harms. Researchers describe the exercises as used for habilitation and rehabilitation of the voice.[3] Anyone with a voice disorder is generally directed by clinicians to a speech-language pathologist.

lead: Straw phonation is an exercise in which a person produces voiced sound through a narrow straw or tube. It is one of several semi-occluded vocal tract (SOVT) exercises, which partly obstruct the mouth opening during phonation, and its use in voice training and therapy has grown over roughly two decades.[3]

Research has measured its immediate effects on vocal tract and glottal function, aerodynamic and electroglottographic parameters, and its use in therapy programmes for dysphonia and vocal fatigue.[1][2][4][7] These studies address voice quality and function rather than perceived attractiveness or authority, which communities interested in voice looksmaxxing sometimes discuss.

paras: SOVT exercises include phonating into straws or tubes, lip trills and tongue trills; much of the research has used straw phonation, and comparisons have measured the intraoral pressures of thirteen different semi-occluding gestures.[3][4]

Imaging work in a single trained singer used computed tomography to compare vocal tract and glottal measures during and after phonation into a tube and a narrow straw.[1] A prospective case series of four singers measured aerodynamic and electroglottographic changes immediately after straw phonation, lip trill and tongue trill.[4]

A study of patients with dysphonia compared three SOVT therapy programmes, lip trill, water-resistance therapy and straw phonation; its authors noted that immediate effects were well established but that the effect of multi-session programmes had been less confirmed.[2] Other studies examined immediate acoustic effects in dysphonic voices, effects on vocal fatigue, lingering effects after exercise, and a comparison of two SOVT training programmes in future occupational voice users.[7][8][9][10]
No identified study tested straw phonation for perceived vocal attractiveness or pitch change.
